en: The Ornament of Clear Realization (*Abhisamayālaṃkāra*).
Homage to Mañjuśrī, the Youthful!
Composed by the noble protector Maitreya, this is the treatise on the instruction of the Perfection of Wisdom titled *The Ornament of Clear Realization*.
The First Chapter: On the Knowledge of All Aspects.
Homage: She who, through omniscience, leads the Śrāvakas seeking peace to tranquility;

Homage to the Mother of the Buddha, who, together with the hosts of Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas, is endowed with that knowledge of the paths which accomplishes the welfare of the world for those who act for the benefit of living beings, and by means of which the Sages perceive this entire universe in all its aspects. (Asa 1.1)
The purpose for undertaking this treatise is this: "The wise should behold that path to omniscience which has been taught here by the Teacher, a path untouched by others. (I.2)
Having established the meaning of the Sūtra within their memory, they may practice the tenfold course of Dharma with ease; this is the purpose of the undertaking. (Asa 1.3)
The establishment of the body of the perfection of wisdom is proclaimed through eight categories of meaning:
the knowledge of all aspects, the knowledge of the paths, and then the knowledge of all things. (Asa 1.4)
The complete awakening in all its aspects, the culminating stage, the serial [awakening], the awakening in a single moment, and the dharma-body—these are the eightfold [stages]. Asa_1.5 //
The production of the thought of enlightenment, instruction, the fourfold limb of penetration, and the basis of practice, which has the dharmadhātu as its intrinsic nature. (I.6)

The objective support, the aim, the acts of donning armor and setting out, the accumulations together with the departure—these constitute the omniscience of all aspects belonging to the Sage. (Asa 1.7)

The path of seeing, which possesses great benefits through its worldly and otherworldly virtues, consists of the acts of darkening and so forth, as well as the paths of the disciple and the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddha]. (Asa 1.8)
Function, resolute belief, and the states of being praised, extolled, and lauded;
the two unsurpassed mental attentions regarding dedication and sympathetic joy. (I.9)
Accomplishment and ultimate purity—this is the path of cultivation for wise Bodhisattvas; thus is the knowledge of the paths proclaimed. (Asa 1.10)
Through wisdom there is no abiding in existence; through compassion there is no dwelling in peace.
Without skillful means there is distance [from enlightenment]; with skillful means there is no distance. (Asa 1.11)

The path of seeing of the Śrāvakas and others is held to be omniscience [in that limited sense] when it consists of the discordant factors and their antidotes, the application, and its equality. (1.12)
The aspects, along with their applications; the virtues and faults with their characteristics;
the stages conducive to liberation and penetration; the learner; and the irreversible assembly. (I.13)
Equanimity toward both existence and peace, the supreme purification of the field, and the complete awakening in all its aspects—this is [the path] together with skillful means. (Asa 1.14)
Its sign, its increase, its firm establishment, and the stability of the mind;
these are the fourfold counteragents to the fourfold conceptualization. (Asa 1.15)
On each of the two paths known as seeing and meditation, there is the uninterrupted concentration along with the obstacles. (1.16)
The realization of the summit is threefold, and the gradual [realization] is tenfold;
the realization in a single moment is fourfold by way of its characteristics. (1.17)
The essential body, the enjoyment body, and likewise the other, the emanation body—the Dharma body together with its activity is thus proclaimed to be fourfold. (1.18)

The first [topic], the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*): the production of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) is the desire for perfect awakening (*samyaksambodhi*) for the sake of others.
And that [perfection] is explained both in brief and in detail, according to the sūtras, as follows: // Asa_1.19 //
By means of earth, gold, the moon, and fire; by treasuries, jewel-mines, and oceans;
by diamonds, mountains, medicinal herbs, and friends; and by the wish-fulfilling gem, the sun, and songs. (Asa 1.20)
And that [benefit] is of twenty-two kinds: through the king’s treasury, great highways, vehicles, and flowing waters; and through the rivers of joyful speech. (Asa 1.21)
2. Instruction regarding practice, regarding the truths, and regarding the three jewels beginning with the Buddha;
regarding non-attachment, regarding tirelessness, and regarding the complete embrace of the path. (Asa 1.22)
It should be known that instruction consists of ten aspects: regarding the five eyes, the six qualities of superknowledge, the path of seeing, and that which is called the path of cultivation. (1.23)

Those of dull and sharp faculties, those attained through faith and through vision, those who go from family to family, those with one interval, those who attain nirvana in the intermediate state, those who attain it upon rebirth, those who attain it with effort, those who attain it without effort, and those who go to the Akaniṣṭha heaven. (Asa 1.24)

The three types of leapers, those for whom existence is at its peak, those who have abandoned attachment to the realm of form, those who attain peace in this very life, the body-witnesses, and the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddhas]—these constitute the twenty [types of noble beings]. Asa_1.25 //

3. The limb of penetration [is established] by way of its object, its aspect, its causality, and its thorough acquisition, for those noble beings who, according to their respective natures, engage with the association of the four conceptualizations. (Asa 1.26)

The superiority of the [levels of] heat and so forth—whether weak, middling, or intense—belonging to the protecting Bodhisattva, over those Śrāvakas who possess the sword [of the path], is established. (1.27)
The object of focus consists of impermanence and so forth, based upon the truths and having their form;
it is the negation of dogmatic adherence and the like, serving as the cause for attaining the three vehicles. (1.28)

The coming and going, the departure and abiding, and the inexpressibility of designation regarding form and the other [aggregates]—their abiding as form and so forth is their lack of intrinsic nature by virtue of that very state. (1.29)
The mutual intrinsic nature of those two is the non-establishment of their impermanence and so forth;
the emptiness of their being that [nature] is the mutual intrinsic nature of these two. (1.30)
The non-appropriation of phenomena is the non-contemplation of their signs, and it is the investigation by means of wisdom through the non-perception of everything. (1.31)
The absence of intrinsic nature in form and the rest, the nature of that absence, their non-arising, their non-departure, their purity, and their signlessness. (Asa 1.32)
Non-adherence to those signs, lack of conviction, and the absence of conceptualization;
his meditative concentration, its activity, prediction, and the exhaustion of mentation. (1.33)
The mutual nature of the triad and the non-conceptuality of meditative concentration—
this constitutes the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) according to their degrees of weak, medium, and intense.
The conceptualization of the apprehended object is twofold, by way of the entity itself and its counteragent;
each of these is further divided ninefold according to the distinctions of the mass of delusion and so forth. (1.35)
The grasper is considered to be twofold, having as its basis both substantial entities and designations:
[the former] in the form of an independent self and so forth, and [the latter] by way of dependence upon the aggregates and so on. (1.36)
The teacher of the absence of intrinsic nature and so forth, through such qualities as the non-depression of the mind;
the abandonment of their opposites and the complete adoption [of these qualities]—this is the summary. (Asa 1.37)
4. The support for practice is sixfold: the dharma of realization, the abandonment of the opposites, the application of those two, wisdom together with compassion. (Asa_1.38)
The lineage (gotra) is said to be the foundation for the uniqueness of the disciple, the sequence of activity for the sake of others, and the effortless operation of primordial wisdom. Asa_1.39 //
Since the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is without differentiation, a distinction of spiritual lineages (gotra) is not tenable;
however, that distinction is proclaimed due to the difference between the qualities to be supported. Asa_1.40 //

5. The object of focus is the object of focus; these are all phenomena (dharmas), namely those that are wholesome and so forth, as well as those known as mundane attainments and those considered supramundane. (Asa 1.41)
Dharmas that are with outflows and without outflows, those that are conditioned and unconditioned, those dharmas shared with disciples, and those that are unique to the Sage. (1.42)
6. The Summary:

Regarding the three—supremacy among all beings, the resolve [for awakening], and the attainment through abandonment—the summary of the Self-Existent Ones (the Buddhas) is to be understood by means of these three greatnesses. (Asa_1.43)
7. The Practice of Armor:

That which consists in the comprehensive inclusion of each of the six types [of perfections] beginning with generosity is the practice of armor; it is explained as being composed of six groups of six, as previously described. (Asa_1.44)

8 – The practice of setting forth consists of [the practice] regarding the meditations and formless attainments, generosity and the other perfections, the path, loving-kindness and the other immeasurables,
the yoga of non-apprehension, and the purifications of the three spheres. (Asa 1.45)
In the summary, in the six superknowledges, and in the method of the knowledge of all aspects, the practice of setting out is to be known as that which mounts the Great Vehicle. (1.46)
9. The practice of the accumulations consists of compassion, the sixfold group beginning with generosity, calm abiding together with insight, the path of union, and skillfulness in means. (I.47)
Knowledge, merit, the path, the dhāraṇīs, and the ten stages; as well as the counteractive measures—these should be known as the sequence of the practice of the accumulations. (I.48) 1.
The Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi).
The first stage is attained through tenfold preparation: [the cultivation of] intention, the state of being a beneficial thing, and equanimity toward all sentient beings. (Asa 1.49)
Generosity, service to friends, seeking the foundation of the true Dharma, constant state of mind directed toward renunciation, and longing for the body of a Buddha. (Asa 1.50)
The teaching of the Dharma is intended as the tenth statement, which is truth;
and their purification should be understood through the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature. This is the Stainless Stage (Vimalā-bhūmi).
Ethical discipline, gratitude, patience, great joy, vast compassion,
reverence, service to the teacher, and eighthly, vigor in giving and the other perfections— [these are the qualities of] the third stage, the Radiant (Prabhākarī).
Insatiability in hearing the Dharma, giving without worldly motive, the complete purification of the Buddha-field, and tirelessness regarding cyclic existence. (Asa 1.53)
Moral shame and dread of blame—these fivefold qualities consist of reflection; [this is] the Radiant Stage (Arciṣmatī). [The practices are:
forest-dwelling, fewness of desires, contentment, and the cultivation of the ascetic purifications and austerities. Asa_1.54 //

Not abandoning the training, loathing sensual desires, world-weariness, renouncing all existing things, being undaunted, and being without expectation—this is the stage of "Very Difficult to Conquer" (Sudurjayā). Asa_1.55. 5. Sudurjayā Bhūmiḥ.
Familiarity, stinginess regarding one's family, places that lead to social distraction, self-exaltation, and contempt for others—
these are the ten unwholesome paths of action. (Asa 1.56)
By abandoning pride, arrogance, error, doubt, and the endurance of afflictions, one attains these ten [qualities] on the fifth stage, the Abhimukhī (the Facing) stage. Asa_1.57 // 6.
Abhimukhī Bhūmiḥ.

Through the complete fulfillment of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom, he is one who avoids the minds of those who desire the state of a disciple, a rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddha], or fear. Asa_1.58 //
Being entreated, he is not dejected; even when asked to give up everything, he is not troubled at heart;
though emaciated, he does not reject those who seek his help—he attains the sixth stage. This is the Dūraṅgamā (Far-Going) Bhūmi.

The grasping at a self and a sentient being, the views of a living soul, a person, annihilationism, and eternalism; [these arise] with respect to signs and causes, and with respect to the aggregates, the elements, and the sense-bases. (Asa 1.60)
Establishment in the three realms, attachment, and a mind that is cowed; and the adherence to views regarding the Three Jewels and the precepts. (Asa 1.61)
He for whom the twenty stains—consisting of disputes regarding emptiness and opposition to it—are severed, reaches the seventh stage. (Asa 1.62)
The knowledge of the three gates of liberation, the purity of the three spheres, compassion without conceit, and the knowledge of the single principle of the equality of all phenomena. (1.63)
The knowledge of receptivity to non-arising is the simultaneous comprehension of all phenomena;
it is the total eradication of conceptual construction and the abandonment of perceptions, views, and afflictions. (I.64)
The settling of the mind in calm abiding, skill in insight, the taming of the mind, and knowledge that is unimpeded everywhere. (1.65)

The absence of attachment, moving at will to other fields simultaneously, and the perception of one's own self-nature everywhere—these constitute the twenty [qualities] of the Immovable Stage (acalā bhūmi). Asa_1.66 // 8. The Immovable Stage.
The knowledge of the minds of all beings, the play of the superknowledges, the auspicious accomplishment of the Buddha-field, and the service to and examination of the Buddhas. (Asa 1.67)
Sensory cognition, the purification of the Buddha-field, abiding like an illusion,
and the intentional taking up of existence— this eightfold activity is proclaimed [on the ninth stage]. This is the stage Sādhumatī (The Good Intelligence).
The infinite aspirations, the knowledge of the cries of gods and others, eloquence like a flowing river, and the supreme descent into the womb. Asa_1.69 //
Regarding lineage, caste, clan, retinue, and birth;

regarding the renunciation, the tree of enlightenment, the abundance of qualities, and one's own perfections—this is the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā-bhūmi). Asa_1.70. 10. The Cloud of Dharma Stage.
Having transcended the nine stages, one is established in the stage of a Buddha;
that by which this is known is to be understood as the tenth bodhisattva stage. (Asa 1.71)

[The equipment of the antidote: The antidote should be known as eightfold on the paths of seeing and cultivation, for the sake of pacifying the eight conceptualizations of the grasped and the grasper. (1.72)
20 – The practice of departure consists in [the absence of effort] regarding the objective, equality, the welfare of sentient beings, and the avoidance of exertion;
it is the ultimate departure, characterized by attainment. (Asa_1.73)
And the departure into the knowledge of all aspects has the path as its domain;
this eightfold nature is to be known as the practice of departure. (Asa 1.74)
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, the treatise of instruction on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Chapter Two: The Knowledge of the Path.
1. [The powers] beginning with "darkening" (*dhyāmīkaraṇatā*):
darkening is [the power] to render the gods' capacity [for perception] obscure by means of one's own radiance;
its object is restricted, its pervasion is universal, and its nature and function are as follows. (Asa 2.1)
2. The Path of the Śrāvakas:
This path of the śrāvakas is to be known, according to the system of the Knowledge of the Path, as the non-apprehension of the aspects of the four noble truths. (Asa_2.2)

Because the aggregates, such as form, are empty and because there is no differentiation among the types of emptiness, the "heat" stage is attained; the "summit" stage is considered to consist in the non-apprehension of those same aggregates. Asa_2.3.
The patiences [are established] therein by way of negating the abiding in the application of permanence and so forth;
the ten stages (bhūmis) are taught in detail starting from the first stage. Asa_2.4.
It is declared that [the stage] consisting of the supreme mundane dharmas belongs to the path of the noble disciples;
for what reason? Because the Buddha, having awakened, does not perceive [any] phenomena as [ultimately] real. (Asa 2.5)
3. The path of the pratyekabuddhas is characterized by the uselessness of instruction from others due to their self-awakening;
and the profundity of the knowledge of the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddhas] is proclaimed. (Asa_2.6)

For whatever purpose, wherever, and in whatever manner service is rendered, that very purpose—though it may not have a pleasant reputation—becomes known in that very same way to each respective person. (Asa 2.7)

The summary of the rhinoceros-like path (khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa-mārga) is to be understood through the abandonment of the conceptualization of the apprehended object, the non-abandonment of the apprehending subject, and its basis. (Asa 2.8)

The form of indicating the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) without contradicting conventional designation is characterized by the stages of Heat (ūṣmagata) and Summits (mūrdhagata), which are distinguished by the non-abandonment of form and so forth. Asa_2.9.
Through internal emptiness and the others, there is the non-appropriation of form and so forth;
through the aspects of the non-arising of form and so forth, there is the stage of Supreme Mundane Dharmas (kṣānti). Asa_2.10.
4. The path of the Bodhisattva consists of four moments of patience and knowledge for each truth;
this is called the path of seeing within the knowledge of the paths, together with its benefits. (Asa_2.11)

Because there is no relationship of container and contained between suchness and the Buddha, they are not admitted to be identical even by way of synonymy; that is their greatness, which is immeasurability. (Asa 2.12)
The determination of form and so forth as being devoid of any limit or end; for one established in that state of Buddhahood, there is neither grasping nor abandoning, and so forth. (Asa 2.13)
The attainment of emptiness through loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables] is the embracing of buddhahood;
it is the destruction of all afflictions and all diseases. (Asa 2.14)

The tranquility of grasping at nirvāṇa, protection from the Buddhas and so forth, beginning with the non-killing of living beings, [are taught] in the method of the knowledge of all aspects. (Asa_2.15)

Establishing oneself in [the path], establishing sentient beings [therein], and the dedication of generosity and the other perfections toward complete enlightenment—these are the moments of the knowledge of the path (mārgajñatā). (Asa 2.16)
5. The activity of the path of cultivation consists of:
subduing from all sides, which is the complete victory over the afflictions; being invulnerable to assault; and the veneration of the support for enlightenment. (Asa_2.17)
The impure path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) 6—the resolve for the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārgādhimukti):
Resolve should be known as threefold: that which has its own welfare as its object, and that which has the welfare of both oneself and others.
And this [perfection] is held to be exclusively for the sake of others, and each of these three types is considered to be of three kinds.
It is weak, medium, and intense, distinguished by further subdivisions such as "weak-weak" and so forth;
since each of these is again threefold, it is considered to be twenty-seven types in total. (Asa 2.19)

7. Praise, laudation, and eulogy regarding the perfection of wisdom for one who is resolved upon the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) are held to consist of three sets of nine degrees of resolve (adhimokṣa). Asa_2.20.
8. The distinction of dedication: Dedication is its supreme activity;
it has the form of non-apprehension and is characterized by the absence of error. (Asa_2.21)
It is secluded, the sphere of mindfulness whose nature is the flood of a Buddha’s merit;
it possesses skillful means, is signless, and is approved by the Buddhas. (Asa 2.22)
Furthermore, there is another threefold transformation that does not enter the triple world:
it consists of the mild, the middling, and the intense, and its nature is the arising of great merit. (Asa 2.23)
9. Rejoicing in the roots of virtue through both skillful means and non-apprehension;
the cultivation of mental attention consisting of rejoicing is prescribed here. (Asa 2.24)
The untainted path of cultivation (10) consists of: its accomplishment,
its intrinsic nature, its excellence, and the non-conditioning of all that.
The non-apprehension of phenomena and their dedication constitute its great purpose. (Asa 2.25)

11. Ultimate purity, service to the Buddhas, and skillfulness in the means such as giving—these are the causes here for resolute belief; [the following] are the causes for the ruin of the Dharma. (Asa_2.26)
Lack of faith in the profound nature of phenomena due to the influence of Māra, attachment to the aggregates and so forth, and being under the sway of evil friends. (Asa 2.27)
The purity of the fruit is indeed the purity of form and so forth; since these two are non-different and indivisible, it is thus called "purity. (Asa 2.28)

Purification is absolute for the Buddha in every respect, due to his abandonment of the three paths of afflictions and the knowable by those who are disciples, rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddhas], and the sons of the Conqueror. (Asa 2.29)
The path beginning with the soft-soft [grade] is purification in the nine stages, serving as the antidote to the stains beginning with the intense-intense. (Asa 2.30)

The equality of the object of cognition and the means of cognition, as well as that of the path, is intended as the antidote to the three realms; this is established by way of resolving that objection. (Asa 2.31)
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, the treatise on the instruction of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Chapter Three: Omniscience (*Sarvajñatā*).
1. By means of wisdom, there is no abiding in existence; 2. by means of compassion, there is no dwelling in quiescence.
She does not abide on the near shore, nor on the far shore, nor in between the two.
The perfection of wisdom is considered to be the knowledge of the equality of the paths. (Asa 3.1)
3. Distance due to lack of means;
4. Non-distance through means.
That [perfection] is distant because of apprehension accompanied by signs due to a lack of means.
Through skill in means, its correct proximity has been described. (Asa 3.2)

5. The adverse factor (*vipakṣa*) consists in the notion of "practice" regarding the emptiness of the aggregates such as form, regarding phenomena belonging to the three times, and regarding the factors conducive to enlightenment such as generosity. (Asa 3.3)
6 – The antidote consists of the absence of egoism regarding generosity and the other perfections, as well as the enjoining of others to them.
This is the negation of attachment; yet, attachment even toward the Victors and so forth is subtle. *Asa_3.4*

That profundity arises from the very nature of discerning the path of phenomena; it is the knowledge that all phenomena are of a single essence, which consists in the avoidance of attachment. Asa_3.5 //
By the negation of being seen and so forth, its difficulty of comprehension is declared;
because it is not cognized through form and the other [sensory objects], its inconceivability is maintained. (3.6)
Having done so, this entire classification of the discordant factors and their antidotes is to be understood exactly as described in the system of omniscience. (Asa 3.7)

Application consists in the negation of [the notion of] form and so forth, of their impermanence and so forth, of their being incomplete or complete, and of their being unattached, with respect to practice. (Asa_3.8)
It is unchanging and not an agent; its application is difficult in three ways.
Yet, because it yields fruit according to one's capacity, it is considered fruitful and desirable. (Asa 3.9)
He who is independent of others and who proclaims the sevenfold [emptiness]—
his fourfold non-conceptualization regarding the equality of form and so forth is considered "equality. (3.10)
9. The path of seeing consists of the moments of receptivity and knowledge regarding the cognition of phenomena and subsequent cognition;
this is the path of seeing concerning the truths of suffering and so forth, the method for attaining omniscience. (Asa_3.11)
Form is neither permanent nor impermanent; it is pure at its ultimate limit.
It is unarisen and unceasing from the beginning, resembling space and free from all taints. (Asa 3.12)
It is free from grasping and, by its very nature, beyond verbal expression;
for its meaning cannot be conveyed to others through speech. (3.13)

Non-apprehension brings about ultimate purity and the non-occurrence of disease; through the cessation of the lower realms and the absence of conceptualization, there is the direct realization of the fruit. (Asa 3.14)
Non-association with signs regarding both the entity and the expression, and the non-arising of cognition—these are the moments of omniscience. (Asa 3.15)
Thus, this very [perfection], again this very [perfection], indeed this very [perfection]—in these three ways, the completion of the three subjects has been fully elucidated. (Asa 3.16)
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, the treatise of instruction on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Chapter Four: The Complete Realization of All Aspects.
Section One: The Aspects.
The definition of "aspects" (ākāra) is the modes of the cognition of things;
because there are three types of omniscience, they are considered to be of exactly three kinds. (Asa 4.1)
Beginning with the aspect of non-existence up to the form of immovability, these four for each truth are recorded as fifteen on the path. (Asa 4.2)
Regarding the cause, the path, suffering, and cessation, they are proclaimed respectively as eight, seven, five, and sixteen. (Asa 4.3)
Beginning with the foundations of mindfulness and ending with the aspects of Buddhahood, these [perfections] belong respectively to the disciples, the bodhisattvas, and the Buddhas. (Asa 4.4)
These are considered to be thirty-seven, thirty-four, and thirty-nine, according to the division into the three types of omniscience, in accordance with the Truth of the Path. (Asa 4.5)
Those who have performed their duties toward the Buddhas, who have planted roots of merit under them, and who are protected by virtuous friends, are the vessels for hearing this [teaching]. (Asa 4.6)

Through the practice of honoring the Buddha, inquiring [about the Dharma], and [observing] the conduct of giving, morality, and so forth, one is considered by the virtuous to be a fit vessel for receiving, retaining, and [applying] the teachings. Asa_4.7 //
2. [The practice] consists of:
because of not abiding in form and so forth; because of the prohibition of yoga with respect to them;
because of the profundity of their suchness; and because of their being difficult to fathom. (Asa_4.8)
Because of the lack of authority in that [other teaching], awakening occurs only with great difficulty and after a long time;
likewise regarding the prediction, the state of being irreversible, and the departure [from saṃsāra] along with its uninterrupted continuity. (Asa 4.9)
[The bodhisattva] is near to enlightenment and swift in the welfare of others because there is neither increase nor decrease;
and because there is no perception of dharma or non-dharma, nor perception of form, the inconceivable, and so forth. (Asa 4.10)
It is non-conceptual regarding form and so forth, their causes, and their existence;
it bestows the jewel of the fruit; it is pure, and it has a limit. (Asa 4.11)
3. Qualities (*guṇa*): The qualities of the Māras consist of fourteen types, such as the impairment of power (*śaktihāni*) and so forth.
4. Faults (*doṣa*).
And the six defects should be understood along with the four sets of ten.
5. Characteristics (lakṣaṇa): That by which something is characterized is to be known as a characteristic, and it is threefold:
knowledge (jñāna), distinction (viśeṣa), activity (kāritra), and that intrinsic nature (svabhāva) which is characterized. (Asa 4.13)

Thus, upon the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, and because the world is of a nature subject to dissolution, regarding the mental activities of sentient beings—their contraction and their outward wandering—(the Buddha’s knowledge is unimpeded). Asa_4.14 //
And in the inexhaustible nature, in the pervasive [states] such as "with passion," in the great and immeasurable, and in consciousness that is non-manifest; (Asa 4.15)
And regarding the knowledge of the invisible mind, there is that which is designated as "opening" (unmiñja) and so forth;
thereafter follows the knowledge of those [minds] by way of the aspect of suchness (tathatā). (Asa 4.16)
This exposition of the Sage’s awakening to suchness is the summary of the characteristics of knowledge, presented under the heading of omniscience. (Asa 4.17)
In emptiness, in the signless, and in that which is devoid of aspiration;
in non-arising, non-ceasing, and so forth, and in the unshakeable nature of phenomena (dharmatā). Asa_4.18.

In the section on the Knowledge of the Path (mārgajñatā), the characteristic of knowledge is intended with respect to the unconditioned, the non-conceptual, and the absence of differentiation and defining marks. (Asa 4.19)

Relying upon one's own duty (svadharma), [one should practice] toward that [teacher] in the monastery, in honoring him, in regarding him as a guru, in showing him respect, and in performing acts of worship for him. (Asa 4.20)
Knowledge that possesses a universal range of activity reveals the unseen;
it is the eye that indicates and makes known the world’s form of emptiness. (Asa 4.21)
The vision of inconceivable peace and the cessation of worldly perceptions is said to be the characteristic of gnosis in the system of the knowledge of all aspects. (Asa 4.22)
The characteristic of excellence is taught through six and ten moments, distinguished by qualities such as inconceivability and so forth, which have the truths as their object. (Asa 4.23)

Inconceivability and incomparability are the transcendence of the measurable and the numerable; they comprise all the noble ones and constitute the uncommon knowledge cognizable by the wise. (Asa 4.24)
The swiftness of wisdom, deficiency and fulfillment, the practice, the realization, the common objective support, completeness, and full acquisition. (Asa 4.25)
And the absence of relishing is to be known as the sixteenfold excellence;
it is the path of excellence by which one is distinguished from other paths. (Asa 4.26)
He is the benefit, the happiness, the protection, the refuge, the shelter, the ultimate resort, the island, and the one designated as the leader for humanity. (Asa 4.27)
Spontaneous, consisting in the non-realization of fruits through the three vehicles—this is the final activity, which is the characteristic of activity. (Asa 4.28)
The signs of the afflictions and their characteristics, the discordant factors and their remedies, seclusion, the difficult task, solitude, the objective, and non-apprehension. (Asa 4.29)

That which is attachment to the prohibited, that which is designated as an objective support, that which is erroneous cognition, and that which is non-obstructive—these are without basis, without coming, and without birth. (Asa 4.30)
The non-apprehension of suchness and its sixteenfold nature, as well as the fact that it is characterized like a characteristic—this is considered the fourth characteristic. (Asa 4.31)
6. The factor conducive to liberation (mokṣabhāgīya) is skill in the complete attainment of signless giving and so forth;
this is held to be the factor conducive to liberation within this realization of all aspects. (Asa_4.32)

Faith has the Buddha and others as its object; vigor has the sphere of giving and so forth as its domain; mindfulness is the perfection of intention; and meditative concentration is non-conceptuality. (Asa 4.33)
Wisdom regarding all phenomena in all their aspects is called *prajñā*; it is fivefold.
Perfect awakening is considered easy to realize by those with sharp faculties, but difficult to realize by those with dull faculties. (Asa 4.34)

7. The object conducive to penetration is all sentient beings; this is praised here as "heat. Its aspects, such as equanimity of mind and so forth, are taught as tenfold with respect to those very beings. (Asa 4.35)

For one who has personally desisted from evil and is established in giving and other virtues, there is the enjoining of these two upon others, as well as speaking in praise of them in a manner that is conducive [to their practice]. (Asa 4.36)

The Summits (mūrdhan) are characterized by their own and others' support, as is the knowledge of truth and likewise forbearance; the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (agradharma) are to be understood through such means as the ripening of sentient beings. (Asa 4.37)
8. The irreversible assembly:
Taking up the factors of penetration within the paths of seeing and cultivation, those bodhisattvas who abide therein constitute the irreversible assembly here. (Asa_4.38)
Through the twenty signs, such as the turning away from form and so forth, which have been determined, this is the definition of the state sharpened by the limbs of penetration. (Asa 4.39)
Turning away from form and the rest, the destruction of doubt and the momentary [nature of] things, one's own abiding in the wholesome, and the enjoining of others to that same state. (Asa 4.40)
Generosity and the other perfections are dependent on others; lack of longing even for profound meanings;
friendliness; non-association with body and so forth; and [non-association] with the fivefold obscuration. (4.41)
The abandonment of all latent tendencies, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and purity;
the robes and so forth [become pure], and worms do not arise in the body. (Asa 4.42)

Absence of crookedness in mind, undertaking of the ascetic practices (dhūta), freedom from envy and the like, proceeding in accordance with the nature of reality (dharmatā), and seeking even the hells for the sake of the world. (Asa 4.43)
Not being led astray by others, recognizing as "Māra" anyone who teaches another path, and awakening to that very fact—this is the conduct approved by the Buddhas. (Asa 4.44)
Established in the stages of heat, summits, patience, and the supreme mundane dharmas, one does not turn back from perfect enlightenment because of these twenty signs. (Asa 4.45)

The six moments of receptivity and knowledge, as well as five and five [moments] in the path of seeing—these are to be understood as the characteristics of a Bodhisattva who is irreversible. (Asa 4.46)
The turning away from perceptions of form and so forth, firmness of mind, the withdrawal from the two inferior vehicles, and the complete exhaustion of the factors of dhyāna and the rest. Asa_4.47 //
Lightness of body and mind, skillful means for the enjoyment of desires, constant practice of celibacy, and complete purity of livelihood. (Asa 4.48)

In the aggregates and so forth, in obstacles, in the accumulations, in the sense faculties and so forth, in battle, and in stinginess and so forth—there is no [application] in the case of application and devoted application. (Asa 4.49)
The negation of dwelling, the non-apprehension of even the subtlest dharma, certainty regarding one's own level, and abiding in the three levels. (Asa 4.50)
The sacrifice of life for the sake of the Dharma—these sixteen moments are the signs of irreversibility for the wise one established on the path of seeing. (Asa 4.51)
The path of cultivation is profound; its profundity consists of emptiness and so forth.
That profundity is the state of being free from the extremes of superimposition and denial. (Asa 4.52)
Reflection, weighing, and profound contemplation constitute the path of cultivation repeatedly;
they occur within the factors of penetration, on the path of seeing, and indeed on the path of cultivation itself. (Asa 4.53)
Because it is continuous, this [cultivation] is considered to be ninefold in its modes;
furthermore, it is divided into the categories of weak, medium, and intense, each of which is further subdivided into weak and so forth. Asa_4.54 //
Designations such as "incalculable" and so forth are not tenable from the perspective of ultimate truth;
they are accepted by the Sage only conventionally, as being the natural outflow of compassion.
Decrease and increase are not applicable to a thing that is beyond verbal expression.
What has been diminished by the path called "cultivation," and what has been acquired? (Asa 4.56)
Just as awakening is, so too is this [attainment] the accomplisher of the desired goal;
awakening has the characteristic of suchness, and that [attainment] is also considered to have that same characteristic. (Asa 4.57)
Awakening is not joined with a preceding mind, nor with a succeeding one;
through the application of the analogy of the lamp, the profound nature of phenomena is eightfold. (Asa_4.58)
There is profundity regarding arising and cessation, regarding suchness, regarding the object of knowledge and knowledge, regarding conduct, and regarding non-dual skill in means. (Asa 4.59)

9. The equality of existence and peace, because all phenomena are like a dream, is the non-conceptualization of existence and peace; the refutations of objections regarding the non-existence of karma and so forth have been stated as above. (Asa_4.60)
10. Supreme purification of the field is the purification of the impurity of the world of sentient beings by means of offering that purification;
likewise, it is the purity of the Buddha-field as the receptacle-world. (Asa_4.61)
11. Skillful means is the domain of this practice; it is the transcending of adversaries. It is non-abiding, according to its penetration, and characterized by being uncommon. (Asa 4.62)
Non-attachment, non-apprehension, being free from signs and aspirations, its characteristic, and the immeasurables—these are the ten forms of skill in means. (Asa 4.63)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, the treatise of instruction on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The Fifth Chapter: The Culminating Realization (Mūrdhābhisamaya).
1. The Signs (liṅga): [The application of the stage of Heat (ūṣman) and the Peak (mūrdhan)] consists of seeing all phenomena as appearing like dreams even within a dream, and so forth.
The signs of yoga that has reached the summit are considered to be twelvefold. (Asa 5.1)
2. Increase (the summit, the application of the summit):
Having made various analogies regarding the measure of the people of Jambudvīpa, the worship of Buddhas, merit, and so forth, increase consists of sixteen aspects. (Asa_5.2)
3. Firm Establishment (*nirūḍhi*): [This consists of] the receptivity (*kṣānti*) and the application of the summits (*mūrdhaprayoga*).
It is the unsurpassed fulfillment of the dharmas of the three types of omniscience; firm establishment is said to be that which does not abandon the welfare of sentient beings. (Asa_5.3)
4. The stabilization of the mind (known as the supreme mundane dharmas; the peak application):

Having performed [meritorious deeds] equal in magnitude to a thousandfold world-system of four continents or a second-order thousandfold world-system, the samādhi is proclaimed by virtue of its great abundance of merit. (Asa_5.4)
5. On the path of seeing (darśanamārga), specifically the practice of the summit (mūrdhaprayoga):
In both [the process of] proceeding and [the process of] ceasing, each consists of nine types.
These two conceptualizations regarding the apprehended object (grāhya-vikalpa) should be known as having the nature of objects that do not correspond to reality. (Asa_5.5)
The conceptualizations of a substantially existent being and a nominally existent being are considered to be the two types of grasping subjects;
these two are each ninefold, according to the distinction between ordinary beings and noble ones.
If those two objects are not thus apprehended, for whom could they be considered apprehenders?
Thus, their characteristic is emptiness by way of the state of being an apprehender. (Asa 5.7)

This [is the summary] regarding intrinsic nature and the lineage, the practice and its full attainment, the object of knowledge and its non-delusion, and the counteractive factors and their opposites. (5.8)
Regarding one's own attainment, the agent, his activity, and the fruit of that action—conceptualization based on the side of engagement is considered to be ninefold. (Asa 5.9)
Because it causes one to fall into the peace of existence, because of the deficiency in realization, because of the absence of support, and because of the impairment in the path; (Asa 5.10)
Regarding the state of being directed toward others, the cessation of that which was aimed at, partiality, and manifoldness; and regarding delusion concerning the place and the departure. (Asa 5.11)
And "in following behind"—this ninefold conceptualization has as its basis the side of cessation and arises from the minds of the Śrāvakas and others. (Asa 5.12)
The first is to be known as the grasper (grāhaka) in the grasping and releasing [of objects], in the mental attention (manaskriyā), and in the conjunction of the three elements (dhātu). (Asa 5.13)

Regarding the locus, adherence, and the designation of the entity of phenomena; regarding attachment and its antidote; and according to one's wish, as well as the destruction of rebirth—[these are the purposes]. (Asa 5.14)

Regarding the non-emergence according to the teaching, the determination of what is and is not the path, cessation along with origination, and the conjunction and disjunction with the objective basis; Asa_5.15 //
In the case of the place, the lineage, destruction, prayer, the absence of causes, and the perception of an adversary, there is another conceptualization which is the grasper. (Asa 5.16)
The manifestation of others in enlightenment, the entrustment for that purpose, and the cause immediately preceding its attainment, characterized by an abundance of merit; (Asa 5.17)

Awakening is said to be the knowledge of the destruction and non-arising of the defilements; for these two occur respectively because of the absence of destruction and the absence of arising with respect to the objects of knowledge. (Asa 5.18)

When primordial nature (prakṛti) has not been restrained by the path called vision, how could the multitude of conceptual constructions be destroyed, or how could they have attained non-arising? (Asa 5.19)
That the existence of phenomena and the destruction of obscurations regarding the knowable are said by others to belong to the Teacher—this is what causes me wonder. (Asa 5.20)
Nothing is to be removed from this, and nothing at all is to be added;
reality is to be seen as it truly is, and he who sees reality is liberated. (Asa 5.21)
The mutual inclusion of each one of those [perfections] within giving and the others, occurring in a single moment and comprised of patience, is here the path of vision. (5.22)
Having entered that samādhi, he then contemplates dependent origination in both forward and reverse order, as the "lion's yawn."
6. The Path of Cultivation (the Culminating Application):

Taking the non-concentrated consciousness belonging to the desire realm as its object, one proceeds by way of entering and emerging from the nine meditative attainments, including cessation, in two ways. (Asa 5.24)
By skipping over one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, or eight [stations], there is the attainment by leaping, which is without cessation and incomparable. (Asa 5.25)

Regarding the concise and the detailed, regarding being unassisted by the Buddhas and not being taken under their care, and regarding the absence of qualities throughout the three times— on these three paths to the supreme good, [the wise do not rely on others].
This first conceptualization of the apprehended object has the aspect of application as its domain;
the second is considered the sphere of activity for the mind and mental factors. (Asa 5.27)
The non-arising of the mind is the lack of mental attention toward the seat of enlightenment;
it is the mental attention toward the Lesser Vehicle and the lack of mental attention toward perfect enlightenment. (Asa 5.28)

On the path of cultivation, conceptual construction should be understood as being fourfold: regarding existence and non-existence, and their respective opposites, as well as that which is unreal. (Asa 5.29)
The first grasper should be known as having the conceptual designation of a sentient being as its object;
it consists of the investigation of attachment to the emptiness of phenomena. (Asa 5.30)

It is proclaimed [as an offense] when a material object has been prepared, regarding the three vehicles, or when there is impurity in the sacrificial gift (dakṣiṇā) or a violation of the conduct (caryā). (Asa 5.31)

The other [obstacles] are ninefold, having as their objects the designation of the sentient being and its causes; they are connected to the path of cultivation because they are the adversaries that obstruct it. (Asa 5.32)

Regarding the three types of omniscience, there is [the obstruction] corresponding to each in their respective threefold obscurations, concerning the union with and separation from tranquility, the path, suchness, and so forth. (5.33)
Regarding inequality, suffering and so forth, the nature of the afflictions, and the absence of duality—in delusion concerning these, the final conceptualization is held to occur. (Asa 5.34)
When these [faults] have been exhausted, the perfections of qualities—which accomplish the happiness of the world in all its aspects—will, as it were, breathe a long sigh of relief. (Asa 5.35)
All [virtues] resort to that Great Being with their full force, abounding in desired fruits, just as rivers flow toward the great ocean. (Asa 5.36)
7. The uninterrupted concentration (the practice of the summit):

Having established the people of the triple-thousand world system in the attainment of the state of disciples, pratyekabuddhas, and the bodhisattva's path, [he performs] the similes of merit. (Asa_5.37)

Having performed [these deeds], through the abundance of merit, immediately after the attainment of Buddhahood, there is the "uninterrupted" (ānantarya) samādhi; and that is omniscience (sarvākārajñatā). (Asa 5.38)
Its object is non-existence, and mindfulness is considered its dominant influence;
its aspect here is tranquility, for those who dispute with the flow of verbal proliferation. (Asa 5.39)

In the occurrence of the objective support, in the determination of its intrinsic nature, in the knowledge of the omniscience of all aspects, and in the ultimate truth together with the conventional; Asa_5.40.
In the application [of practice], in the three Jewels, in the means, in the Sage’s commitment, in error, in the true path, and in the remedy and its opposite; (5.41)
Regarding the characteristics and the cultivation [of the path], there are six and ten misconceptions held by the proponents concerning the basis of the knowledge of all aspects. (5.42)
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, the treatise of instruction on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The sixth chapter is the Chapter on the Gradual [Path].
It consists of generosity, wisdom, and so forth, up to the recollections of the Buddha and the rest.
The sequential practice is considered to be by way of the intrinsic nature of the non-existence of phenomena.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, the treatise of instruction on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The seventh chapter is the Chapter on Enlightenment in a Single Instant (1):
The Characteristic of Non-Ripening.

Because all uncontaminated phenomena are subsumed even by each single one [of the perfections], this momentary realization of the Sage through generosity and the other [perfections] is to be known. (Asa 7.1)
Just as even a single bucket at a waterwheel, when pulled by men, moves the whole wheel at once, so too does knowledge in a single moment. (Asa 7.2)
2. When the state characterized by maturation—the condition of the nature of maturation—consists entirely of purity, then the Perfection of Wisdom arises as gnosis in a single moment. (Asa_7.3)

3. Having established himself in phenomena that are like dreams and characterized by the absence of marks, he realizes the marklessness of all phenomena in a single instant through the practice of giving and the other perfections. Asa_7.4 //
4. Having the characteristic of non-duality, one does not perceive a dream and the seer of that dream as being joined in duality;
one perceives the non-dual reality of all phenomena in a single instant. (Asa_7.5)
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, the treatise of instruction on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The eighth chapter: The Chapter on the Dharmakāya.
1. The svabhāvakāya consists of those untainted dharmas which have attained purity in all its aspects;
it is the body of the Sage characterized by their intrinsic nature.

2. The knowledge-dharmakāya consists of the factors conducive to awakening, the immeasurables, the liberations in their successive order, the ninefold meditative attainments, and the tenfold totalities. (Asa_8.2)

The bases of mastery are of eight kinds according to their divisions; [then there are] absence of conflict, knowledge resulting from prayer, the superknowledges, and the analytical knowledges. (Asa 8.3)
Then there are the four purities in all their aspects, the ten masteries, the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, and the state of having nothing to guard. Asa_8.4 //

The threefold application of mindfulness, the state of being free from the three kinds of forgetfulness, the complete eradication of latent predispositions, and great compassion for living beings. (Asa 8.5)
The eighteen unique qualities belonging exclusively to the Sage, as well as omniscience—this is designated as the Dharmakāya. (Asa_8.6)
The Śrāvaka possesses the "non-affliction" (araṇā) because he has abandoned human afflictions;
the Victor’s non-affliction exists in villages and other places for the sake of cutting off the stream of those very afflictions. (Asa_8.7)
Effortless, unattached, unimpeded, and ever-present;
the Buddha’s knowledge resulting from his vow is held to be that which dispels all questions. (Asa 8.8)
Whenever and for whomever the cause has reached maturity, he manifests himself to that very person so that their welfare may be accomplished. (Asa 8.9)
For even when the rain-god pours down, a seed does not sprout;
likewise, even upon the appearance of Buddhas, one who lacks the capacity does not enjoy the auspicious fruit.
Thus, because of the vastness of his activity, the Buddha is described as all-pervading;
and because that very [activity] is inexhaustible, he is also said to be eternal. (8.11)
3. This body of the Sage, consisting of the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, is considered the Enjoyment Body (sāmbhogika-kāya), because it experiences the Mahāyāna. (Asa_8.12)
His hands are marked with wheels; his feet are like those of a tortoise; his fingers and toes are joined by a web;
his hands and feet are youthful and soft; and his body is endowed with seven prominent features. (Asa 8.13)

He has long fingers, broad heels, and well-proportioned limbs; his body is expansive, straight, with prominent ankles, upward-pointing body hair, shanks like those of the eneya antelope, and arms that reach his knees; his private parts are enclosed in a sheath like those of a noble steed. (Asa 8.14)

He is golden-colored with very fine skin; his body hairs grow individually, turning to the right; his face is marked by a tuft of hair (ūrṇā); his torso is like that of a lion; his shoulders are rounded and the space between them is well-filled. (Asa 8.15)
His inferior taste is renowned as the most excellent of tastes; his body is like a *nyagrodha* tree, equal in its circular proportions;
he has a protuberance on his head (*uṣṇīṣa*), broad and beautiful tongues, the voice of Brahmā, a jaw like a lion’s, and perfectly white [teeth]. Asa_8.16 //
The teeth are equal in size, closely set, and four sets of ten without deficiency;
his eyes are blue, and his eyelashes are like those of a bull—these indeed are the thirty-two marks. (Asa 8.17)
Whichever cause there may be here that accomplishes each respective characteristic, this [Bodhisattva] fulfills it all; such is the characteristic of his complete attainment.
Following after one's gurus and so forth, firmness regarding the vow, gathering [disciples], attending upon them, and the giving of excellent things. (Asa 8.19)
The undertaking of the release of those condemned to death, the increase of the wholesome, and so forth—such is the cause that establishes the [thirty-two] marks, according to the sūtras. (Asa 8.20)
The nails of the Sage are copper-colored, glossy, and prominent; his fingers are rounded, well-defined, and tapering; and his veins are hidden and without knots. (Asa 8.21)
The ankles are hidden, the feet are even, and like those of a lion, an elephant, a twice-born, or a lord of cattle;
his stride is courageous, his gait is beautiful, and his limbs are straight and well-rounded. (Asa 8.22)
The hands and feet are well-proportioned, the skin is pure and soft, the limbs are clean, the secondary marks are present, and the body is beautiful with broad, rounded contours. (Asa 8.23)
Evenness of gait, purity of the eyes, delicacy, the state of having limbs that are neither dejected nor over-exalted, and the state of having well-knit limbs. (Asa 8.24)
Well-proportioned limbs, purity of light undimmed by darkness, rounded, polished, unblemished eyes, a slender abdomen, and profound depth. Asa_8.25 //
The navel is clockwise-rotating and beautiful to behold from all sides;
his conduct is pure, and his body is free from black moles. Asa_8.26 //
The hands are as soft as cotton and possess smooth, deep, and long lines;
the face is not overly long, and the lips are like the bimba fruit in their reflection.
The tongue is soft, thin, and red; his voice has the resonance of a thundercloud;
his tone is beautiful and melodious; and his fangs are rounded, sharp, white, and even. (Asa 8.28)
His nose is high and gradually tapering, supremely pure;
his eyes are wide, adorned with eyelashes, and possess the appearance of lotus petals. (Asa 8.29)
His eyebrows and arms are long, smooth, very glossy, and have even hair; his ears are full, long, symmetrical, and free from any defects. (Asa 8.30)
The forehead is unmarred; the head is broad and full; the eyebrows possess a radiant luster, are smooth, and have well-defined, undisturbed forms. Asa_8.31.
The hair of men is not coarse and captivates due to its fragrance;
the Śrīvatsa and the Svastika—these are considered the secondary marks (anuvyañjana) of a Buddha. (Asa 8.32)

4. The Emanation Body (nairmāṇika-kāya) is that by which the Sage performs various benefits for the world equally; until the end of existence, this Emanation Body of the Muni remains uninterrupted. (Asa_8.33)
Likewise, his buddha-activities and his karma are held to be uninterrupted as long as saṃsāra lasts;
his karma consists in the pacification of the realms of existence and in the fourfold means of integration. (Asa 8.34)
[The application of] settling is with respect to the understanding of affliction and purification, the true nature of the welfare of sentient beings, and the six perfections. (Asa 8.35)
In the Buddha-path, in emptiness by its very nature, in the cessation of duality, in convention, in non-apprehension, and in the maturation of embodied beings. (Asa 8.36)
Regarding the prevention of attachment to the path of a bodhisattva, the attainment of awakening, the purification of the Buddha-field, and with respect to certainty; (Asa 8.37)

In the immeasurable benefit for sentient beings, in virtues such as serving the Buddhas, in the factors of enlightenment, in the non-perishing of karmic actions, and in the vision of the truths; Asa_8.38.
And regarding the abandonment of error, the method of its lack of substantial reality, purification along with its equipment, and both the conditioned and the unconditioned; Asa_8.39.
The non-perception of distinctions and the establishment in nirvāṇa:
this is considered the twenty-sevenfold activity of the dharma-body. (Asa 8.40)
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, the treatise of instruction on the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
